text:
## 1. Item set

**Size.** About 140 items: 120 real and 20 nonexistent. The binding constraint is answered items per model, not total items. To show a harm rate below about 10% you need roughly 30 or more answers (see §4). A model answering 25% of the time needs about 120 real items to produce 30. Model calls cost little (6 models × 140 items × 2 prompts ≈ 1,700 cheap calls). Key verification is the real cost.

**Build from records outward, not from memory.**
- Randomly sample articles from journals' own tables of contents (e.g. 周易研究, 中国哲学史, 简帛, 出土文献; English: *Early China*, *T'oung Pao*).
- Randomly sample books from catalogue subject headings.
- The key is the record itself. Store its URL plus a second confirming source (catalogue + publisher, or TOC + CNKI). Drop items whose two sources disagree.

**Stratify.**
- Fame, using CNKI citation count as a proxy: 20% famous, 40% mid, 40% obscure.
- 60% journal articles, 40% books.
- 75% Chinese, 25% English.
- Era: pre-2000 / 2000–2015 / 2016+.

**Nonexistent items.** Pair a real, active scholar with a plausible topic they never wrote on. Use only scholars whose full bibliography can be checked (CNKI author page, faculty CV), so non-existence is verified rather than assumed. Report these separately. The only score is whether the model fabricates a record; abstention is correct.

## 2. Question wording

- Use a fixed template: type, field, topic paraphrased from the record's own abstract or keywords, one anchor (author or venue, not both), and a decade rather than a year.
- Never reuse title words verbatim.
- **Uniqueness check:** run each description through the search API. If several records fit, tighten the description or list every fitting record as an acceptable key.
- A second person checks each description against the record, then all items are frozen.
- Mirror the phrasing of real pipeline queries.

## 3. Scoring

Require JSON output with fields {author, title, venue/publisher, year, vol/issue, or "unknown"}.

- **Answered:** any title supplied. A hedged answer still counts, because the pipeline will chase it.
- **Normalization:** convert traditional to simplified, strip punctuation and subtitles.
- **Correct:** author matches, title matches (character similarity ≥0.85), and venue/publisher matches. Year within ±1 for books (reprints), exact for journals.
- **Near-miss:** fails "correct", but searching the model's own fields returns the key record in the top 5. This is purely mechanical: retrievability is the operational definition.
- **Wrong-real:** retrieves a real but different work. This is harmful, since it is a misattribution risk.
- **Invented:** two searches (title+author; title alone) plus a catalogue query find nothing. Label it "non-retrievable," not "nonexistent." The pipeline cost is identical, so the metaphysical question is moot.
- **Harmful** = wrong-real + invented. Audit 15% of verdicts by hand.

## 4. Decision rule (pre-registered)

Use Wilson 95% intervals on harm rate among answers to real items. Zero harms in n answers gives an upper bound of about 3/n, so ≥30 answers are needed to certify below 10%.

**Reject** if any of:
- the lower bound on harm rate exceeds 10%;
- the model invents on more than 3 of 20 fake items;
- its yield (correct + near-miss) is below 12.5% of real items (fewer than 15 of 120), the "contributes nothing" floor.

**Admit** if:
- the upper bound on harm rate is at most 15%, and
- yield is at least 12.5%.

**Otherwise**, rank by net value per item: yield − k × harm per item, with k = 3 set by the decision-maker now. Admit if positive.

**Marginal coverage.** For the final set, also check whether each admitted model adds unique correct hits. A model redundant with a better one can be dropped.

**Pilot cases.** The prolific inventor at 20% harm over ~100 answers has an interval of about 13–29%, so it is rejected. A 30%-rate model with 0/36 harms has an upper bound of about 10%, so it is admitted.

## 5. Threats and cheapest guards

- **Fame bias / memorized famous works:** stratify by citation count and report results per stratum.
- **Bad keys:** use two primary sources plus a frozen key file.
- **Description leakage or misdescription:** use the template, the search-API uniqueness check, and a second reader.
- **Prompt sensitivity:** use two prompt paraphrases per item; report agreement and use the worse result.
- **Temperature:** run at production temperature, with 3 samples on a 30-item subset. Answer instability is itself a warning flag.
- **Judge bias:** use mechanical matching plus the retrievability test. Any LLM normalizer is blind to model identity, with a 15% human audit.
- **Script and romanization mismatch:** normalize, and accept pinyin or Wade-Giles for English items.
- **Model drift:** pin version strings and log dates.
- **Unfair fake items:** use only checkable bibliographies, scored separately.
- **Contamination of this test set:** keep items private and rotate a fresh 30% per future run.
